# Page 2^page=2
Abstract The abstract is the first section in a report, but is should be the last to be written. It should contain essential information only and needs to be very concise (200 words maximum). The purpose of the abstract is to summarise the whole the report, including the key findings/outcomes so that the reader can decide whether or not they need to read it in full. The abstract should summarise methodology/procedure, results and conclusions. 2

Include a detailed description of the problem you are trying to solve. State technical objectives clearly. It should be possible for the reader to understand the technical requirements of the assignment without having seen the assignment brief. DO NOT copy-paste from the assignment brief – write a summary in your own words. 5

# Page 7^page=7
Figure 2 Example of an RC timer circuit (Horowitz & Hill, 2015) 2.4 Inserting and formatting formulae Insert evidence of calculations using the built-in Word equation editor or a Word plug-in. x=y/x + c becomes x= y x + c Mathtype is a powerful equation editor, the free demo version is more than adequate for most purposes and can be downloaded from the following link: http://www.dessci.com/en/products/mathtype/ Also consider a numbering scheme for equations so you can refer to them easily in your writing. x=−b ± √b 2−4 ac 2 a (2.1) Having numbered the formula it is possible to now state that equation (2.1) is the quadratic formula. The numbering scheme adopted is chapter number followed by the equation number. This numbering scheme is sensible if you have a large number of equations across several chapters. 2.5 Inserting code snippets/listings Enter code listings using a fixed width font. Here I have used the Code style built into this template which uses the fixed width Consolas font as well as a compact line spacing to make code listings compact and easy to read (see below). void main (void) { cout >> "Hello World"; // Here is some code } Large listings of code should generally be placed in an appendix. 7

# Page 12^page=12
7 References Horowitz, P. & Hill, W. (2005). The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.). Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. All sources must be referenced – failing to do this an academic offence and has serious consequences. University standard is APA 6th edition (similar to Harvard in style). Other referencing styles (e.g. numeric) are acceptable for technical reports, discuss this with your supervisor. The benefit of a style such as APA 6th over a numeric style is that no re-ordering of references is required if the report is edited. The University library has provided some guidance on the APA 6th referencing scheme, available here: https://www.hud.ac.uk/library/finding-info/apa-referencing/ 12

# Page 13^page=13
8 Appendix A Anything which is not a direct and essential part of the narrative should be placed in this section. If it impacts upon the flow of the narrative then put it in an appendix. Examples of items that might be considered for conclusion in an appendix include:  Large tables raw data  Circuit schematics  Code listings  Bill of materials  CAD renderings  PCB layouts Use separate appendices to group similar item. For instance, circuit schematics and PCB layouts might be grouped into Appendix A and Appendix B respectively. 13
